transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-10 10:00 AM PT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jared Kim (Redwood SE), Sofia Martinez (AstraMed - Head of ML), Ethan Ross (AstraMed - Infra Lead), Priya Sharma (AstraMed - PM)

Summary (auto): quick run through of last week's bench numbers, dug into p99 and batching differences vs baseline provider, talked about KV cache and quantization tradeoffs, next steps to run additional p99 tests and schedule canary on dedicated pool.

00:00 Maya (Redwood AE): ok good morning everyone, we are on the hour. thanks for joining the weekly poc sync. quick roll call?
00:10 Sofia (AstraMed): hi this is Sofia, thanks maya.
00:12 Ethan (AstraMed): Ethan here.
00:14 Priya (AstraMed): Priya here.
00:16 Maya: great, Jared from engineering is with me. Jared do you want to kick off with the results deck?
00:20 Jared (Redwood SE): yeah sure, i'll share screen in a sec. so we focused this week on throughput and latency comparisons against your baseline provider using your sample workload. high level first: median latency improved from about 65ms to 42ms and p99 improved from 320ms to 210ms on our hosted config with kv-cache and batching. throughput at target sequence length was about 420 requests/sec vs baseline 300 req/sec. those are approximate.
00:45 Sofia: those numbers look promising. can you clarify sequence length distribution you used? last time baseline had a bunch of long sequences.
00:52 Jared: good point - we used your provided sample but clipped the tail at 1k tokens to match the baseline config, but the histogram was slightly different, there was a 7% heavier tail in your baseline sample. i'll attach the exact histogram row.
01:08 Priya: when you say kv-cache enabled, does that assume prefix reuse? our product has a lot of repeated instruction tokens per session.
01:16 Jared: yes, we measured two modes - cold and warm. warm mode assumes 70% prefix reuse which gives the biggest gains; cold mode numbers are closer to baseline but still slightly better because of our kernel optimizations and continuous batching.
01:30 Sofia: what about quantization? baseline provider said they use q4 and some int8. are you comparing fp16 or quantized?
01:37 Jared: for these runs we used our fp16 path with mixed precision and a model variant quantized to int8 for the production-like runs. we saw a modest accuracy delta on a few eval prompts but within your tolerance per earlier evals. the throughput gains on int8 were +18% vs fp16 in our env.
01:58 Ethan: any differences in p99 tail noise? our ops team cares about spikes. baseline showed occasional p99 spikes up to 600ms during bursts.
02:07 Jared: we collected traces - the spikes often correlated to autoscaler spin-ups on baseline. because we were running on a pinned dedicated-ish pool for the test, spikes were much lower. our p99 spikes hit ~260-300ms during short bursts, but sustained load stayed around 210ms. i'll share the span traces.
02:29 Maya: can i interrupt, just to make sure - are all cost numbers normalized to your committed instance pricing or pay-as-you-go? we need apples-to-apples.
02:36 Jared: we normalized to the same underlying GPU sku and ran unit economics at steady state including batching. the cost per 1M tokens came out about 14% lower on Redwood because of better batching and kv cache hit-rate. note that's assuming your workload hits similar cache reuse.
02:52 Sofia: hmm 14% is interesting. baseline provider says they can do similar with more aggressive batching but they trade latency. how did you balance batching size vs latency?
03:02 Jared: we used dynamic batching with a latency SLO of 120ms for median; for the high throughput test we relaxed to 200ms SLO which increased throughput by ~25%. we can tune per route.
03:18 Priya: were these tests on hosted or dedicated? we might be considering dedicated for compliance.
03:22 Jared: hosted cluster but using reserved nodes to avoid noisy neighbors; behavior on Dedicated should be comparable or slightly better since you control autoscaling and reserved capacity.
03:33 Ethan: on networking - for private deployment we'll need VPC peering and SAML. any blockers?
03:38 Maya: not blockers, we have a standard VPC playbook and SSO/SAML guide; ethan, we can send the infra checklist.
03:44 Ethan: thanks.
03:46 Jared: coming back to numbers, i'll read the table so folks have the raw: baseline median 65ms, baseline p99 320ms, baseline throughput 300 rps. redwood median 42ms, redwood p99 210ms, redwood throughput 420 rps. cost delta -14% at steady state assumptions. kv-cache hit-rate we measured ~68% across sessions which drove a lot of benefit.
04:10 Sofia: ok that's helpful. can you explain how kv-cache behaves with long sessions and partial prompts? we saw some cache invalidations last week with our session routing.
04:20 Jared: sure, our KV cache uses token-level keys per session id; invalidations happen only if the model variant or tokenizer changes. partial prompts still cache prefix states - you get partial reuse. there can be less reuse if you do heavy prompt templating per request.
04:38 Priya: is there perf regression risk when switching model variants for fallbacks? we have fallback policies to smaller models during load.
04:46 Jared: we support automated fallback to compatible variants; we saw a small latency bump during the transition window but our routing minimizes in-flight re-encodings. it's typical to see a 10-15% latency hit during variant swap windows.
04:59 Sofia: one concern - baseline provider cited SOC2 and audit logs as a must. do you have the logs and retention options?
05:06 Maya: yes we have SOC2 org-level compliance; audit logs, retention configurable per enterprise plan. we can send the security pack link.
05:12 Ethan: perfect. also can you share the exact benchmarking script and command line so our infra can replicate?
05:18 Jared: yes i'll push the airflow/runner commands and the docker compose we used to the shared folder. i'll include environment vars, seed, and p99 sampling details.
05:28 Maya: any surprises in the runs? errors, model mismatches?
05:31 Jared: small issue with tokenizer mismatch for one legacy prompt, that created a few outliers; fixed by aligning tokenizer versions. otherwise fairly clean.
05:40 Priya: about the 70% prefix reuse assumption - if our real reuse is lower we might not see the full 14% cost reduction. what would you recommend to mitigate?
05:49 Jared: two levers: 1) increase caching TTL and session affinity on client side, 2) apply lightweight prompt canonicalization to increase reuse. we can provide canonicalization examples.
06:03 Sofia: can we get a p99 run that simulates a 24-hour mixed workload with peak bursts at 10x baseline? that's what ops worried about.
06:12 Jared: yes we can run a long-tail p99 stress test, but it'll take about 48 hours to run and analyze. propose we run it this week and deliver by Friday.
06:21 Maya: timeline-wise that aligns: customer to drop workload samples by Tuesday, we run the p99 stress and share results by next Friday, then schedule canary the week after.
06:30 Sofia: sounds good. one more ask - we'd like the bench spreadsheet with per-request token counts and cost breakouts.
06:36 Jared: i'll update the spreadsheet and attach per-request rows; also include the config snippet for batch sizes and latency SLOs we used.
06:45 Priya: any legal or procurement notes for pilot? we might need a limited data processing addendum.
06:50 Maya: we have a standard pilot MSA + DPA template. i'll send an initial version.
06:54 Ethan: for canary we'd probably want a dedicated small pool behind a feature flag - how fast can you provision?
06:59 Jared: we can provision a dedicated 4-GPU pool within 24-48 hours once the contract is signed and infra creds are provided.
07:08 Sofia: ok that's acceptable.
07:10 Maya: awesome. quick recap: jared runs p99 stress + traces and uploads, may a shares pricing and pilot MSA, sofia uploads workload, ethan confirms VPC window, schedule canary for 7/21. any other items?
07:23 Sofia: no, thanks everyone.
07:25 Priya: thanks.
07:26 Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links. bye.

Action items (auto): see action items field above.
